newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. commander calls U.S. Iraq strikes violations.
newsitem.headline: U.N. commander calls U.S. Iraq strikes violations.

text.p: The United Nations said on Wednesday some U.S. missile attacks on Iraq this month violated the demilitarised zone between Iraq and Kuwait set up by the world body after the Gulf War.

Major General Gian Santillo, Force Commander of the U.N. Iraq-Kuwait Observer Mission (UNIKOM), added that overflights of the zone on Wednesday by unidentified warplanes were also a violation of the sensitive frontier's demilitarised status.
"It does constitute a violation...any military hardware in the DMZ (demilitarised zone) constitutes a violation," Santillo, referring to the flights, told Reuters in an interview.
U.N. observers and Reuters reporters on Wednesday saw two low-flying warplanes enter Kuwait from the north and then turn back and fly over the border into Iraq.
Witnesses said the planes appeared to be Western aircraft participating in patrols of a no-fly zone imposed in southern Iraq by the United States, France and Britain in 1992.

Santillo, an Italian, also said that UNIKOM observers had seen "a number" of the 44 U.S. cruise missiles that were fired at targets in southern Iraq on September 3 and 4 as they flew over the zone on their way north to targets in Iraq.
"It was a violation," Santillo said of the missiles.

Another UNIKOM official said observers had seen about eight of the missiles, registering them as a violation of the boundary's demilitarised status enshrined in U.N. resolutions passed after the Gulf War ended an Iraqi occupation of Kuwait.
The violations were reported to U.N. headquarters in New York, the UNIKOM official said.
The United Nations created the demilitarised border zone in April 1991 and deployed UNIKOM along it to monitor the boundary and help deter any violations of it by either side.
UNIKOM's observers try to ensure that no military activity of any kind occurs in the zone that straddles the 207 km (130 mile)-long land border and 40 km (25 mile)-sea border.
They must also ensure that no military force of any kind is present in the zone, which extends 10 km (six miles) into Iraq and five km (three miles) into Kuwait.

The UNIKOM official said it was impossible to verify the nationality of the forces that fired the eight missiles but added it appeared they were among the 44 launched by the United States as punishment for Iraqi attacks on northern Iraqi Kurds.
"Any overflights over the DMZ (demilitarised zone) by either side, or by their allies, constitutes a violation," said UNIKOM spokesman Saleem Fahmawi.

Fahmawi added that the zone was calm and no other significant military movements had been noticed during the latest flare-up between Washington and Iraq over the enforcement of a Western-imposed no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
Western diplomats said they did not expect a diplomatic indicent over the UNIKOM report, describing it as "theoretical" and said it had not been an issue at U.N. headquarters.
Diplomats said they believed some U.S. missile strikes against Iraq during previous confrontations with Baghdad in 1993 and 1994 had also been reported as violations by UNIKOM.
Diplomats say the no-fly-zone patrols are normally not an issue for UNIKOM because they usually fly too high to be seen by the observers, who rely on the naked eye for surveillance.
